ABSTRACT
Objective: To report an association between two
autoimmune conditions, Graves’ disease and stiff-person
(stiff-man) syndrome, and discuss the relevant literature.
Methods: We present a case of a 52-year-old white
woman with stiff-person syndrome who also had Graves’
disease, discuss her management, and review the related
literature. Pertinent published reports from 1950 through
2004 were researched with use of MEDLINE and
PubMed, and cross-references to other articles were
reviewed.
Results: A 52-year-old white woman presented with
symptoms of hyperthyroidism due to Graves’ disease.
Laboratory data were as follows: thyrotropin <0.005
μIU/mL, thyroxine 11.1 μg/dL, free thyroxine index (FTI)
10.7, and triiodothyronine 170 ng/dL. Thyroid-stimulating
immunoglobulins (TSI) and thyrotropin-binding inhibito-
ry immunoglobulins (TBII) were positive at 1,986% and
82.5 U/L, respectively. The hyperthyroidism was treated
with propranolol. She had a long-standing history of mus-
culoskeletal complaints and was ultimately diagnosed
with stiff-person syndrome. During her thyroid evalua-
tion, she had severe neurologic deterioration that necessi-
tated hospitalization and treatment with clonazepam,
baclofen, intravenous immunoglobulin, and subsequently
prednisone and azathioprine for appreciable symptomatic
relief. The aggressive immunosuppression had a profound
effect on her symptoms of hyperthyroidism, results of thy-
roid function tests, and thyrotropin receptor antibodies
(TRABs). Thyrotropin was 0.52 μIU/mL, thyroxine was
6.9 μg/dL, and FTI was 5.7. The TSI decreased from
1,986% to 248%, and her TBII normalized from 82.5 U/L
to <5 U/L. She was clinically and biochemically euthyroid
at last follow-up in May 2004.
Conclusion: This case illustrates the association
between TRAB-positive Graves’ disease and stiff-person
syndrome and the improvement of Graves’ disease with
immunosuppressive therapy. (Endocr Pract. 2005;11:
259-264)
INTRODUCTION
Graves’ disease is a common autoimmune disorder
with an annual incidence of 80 cases per 100,000 in
women and 10 cases per 100,000 in men (1,2). The iden-
tification of the long-acting thyroid stimulator (LATS)
thyrotropin receptor as the target of the LATS IgG and
demonstration of the presence of thyrotropin receptor anti-
bodies (TRABs) in more than 95% of patients with
Graves’ disease indicate an autoimmune basis. The
strongest direct evidence comes from the stimulation of
thyroid cellular activity in vitro by IgG from patients with
Graves’ disease and the passive transfer of transient
hyperthyroidism to the newborn of an affected pregnant
mother (1,2). Graves’ disease is associated with many
organ-specific autoimmune conditions, including type 1
diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease, vitiligo, pernicious
anemia, myasthenia gravis, and premature ovarian failure
(2,3), as well as autoimmune antibody positivity even in
the absence of overt clinical disease (4-7).
Stiff-person (stiff-man) syndrome (SPS) is a rare neu-
rologic syndrome of unknown cause, characterized by
progressive painful muscle spasms, muscle stiffness, and
muscle rigidity (8,9). SPS is a clinical diagnosis, associat-
ed with positive anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)
antibodies and a suggestive electromyogram (EMG)
(4,10-13). SPS is associated with several autoimmune

diseases, including Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and type 1 dia-
betes (4,10-13), and it is associated with hyperthyroidism.
Although hyperthyroidism due to apparent Graves’ dis-
ease has been described in association with SPS
(10,14,15), TRABs were not measured in those previous
studies.
We report a documented association of Graves’ dis-
ease and SPS in conjunction with TRAB positivity. Our
patient also had biochemical remission of hyperthyroidism
with immunosuppressive therapy for SPS.
CASE REPORT
A 52-year-old right-handed white woman presented
to the endocrine clinic for evaluation of hyperthyroidism.
She had a 9-month history of anxiety, rapid speech, dysp-
nea on exertion, generalized weakness, and tremulousness.
She had no local neck symptoms. She reported intermit-
tent fatigue, mood swings, restless sleep, heat intolerance,
and excessive sweating. She had also noticed palpitations
and had irregular menses. Although her appetite had
increased, she had maintained a stable weight. She had
some eyelid swelling and minimal discomfort. A review of
systems revealed considerable muscle aches and stiffness
in the back and legs, gait difficulties, frequent falls, diffi-
culty climbing stairs, and urinary incontinence. Her histo-
ry revealed hypertension, osteoarthritis with cervical and
lumbar spondylosis, cholecystectomy, and tubal ligation.
She reported a strong family history of Graves’ disease
(sister and first cousin). She was married and had 3 chil-
dren. She denied alcohol or tobacco use. Her drug history
included tolterodine (Detrol), sertraline (Zoloft), baclofen,
and lisinopril.
On physical examination, the patient’s weight was
82.1 kg, height was 165 cm, pulse was 84 beats/min, and
blood pressure was 210/90 mm Hg. She looked anxious,
with a stare, chemosis, and lid lag. The rest of the eye
examination, including exophthalmometry, showed no
other abnormalities. She had fine tremors of the out-
stretched hands; normal findings on thyroid examination;
brisk symmetric reflexes; proximal myopathy; abnormal
gait, almost spastic in nature; and spasm of the anterior
abdominal wall and paraspinal musculature. The rest of
her examination was unremarkable.
Initial thyroid function tests indicated biochemical
hyperthyroidism (Table 1). Radioiodine (
131I) thyroid
uptake was 16% at 4 hours (estimated as 33% at 24 hours),
and the scan showed a homogeneous pattern. TRABs were
positive (Table 1). Thyrotropin-binding inhibitory
immunoglobulins (TBII) were measured by radioreceptor
assay (Kronus, Inc.), and thyroid-stimulating immuno-
globulins (TSI) were measured by a cell bioassay, as
described previously (16). Treatment with propranolol (40
mg three times daily) was initiated.
Before her visit to the endocrine clinic, the patient had
had several consultations with specialists, including a
rheumatologist, spine orthopedist, pulmonologist, and
neurologist. She had an extensive evaluation, including
magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which showed
normal findings, and of the spine, which disclosed moder-
ate cervical and lumbar spondylosis without spinal cord
compromise. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(Westergren), C-reactive protein, serum protein elec-
trophoresis, and rheumatoid factor all demonstrated
normal results. She had normal chest x-ray findings and
restrictive physiology, with normal diffusion lung capaci-

activation of normal motor units of the paraspinal and
proximal lower extremity muscles.
The patient was diagnosed with SPS (elevated anti-
GAD antibody level, 431 nmol/L; normal, ≤0.02 nmol/L).
Treatment with baclofen yielded improvement in painful
spasms, and she had no further falls. Her ambulation was
substantially improved. Three months later, however, she
required hospitalization because of worsening dyspnea,
frequent falls, and increasing painful spasms. She was
treated with clonazepam (Klonopin) but had little
improvement. She received a 5-day course of intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy (400 mg/kg daily). An
echocardiogram showed normal findings, as did computed
tomographic scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
Subsequent improvement allowed her dismissal from the
hospital.
Within a month, deterioration of the patient’s condi-
tion necessitated another 5-day course of IVIG, which
yielded no improvement. She was then treated with a
5-day intravenous course of methylprednisolone at 1
g/day, and dramatic improvement ensued. She continued
with orally administered prednisone in dosages up to 80
mg daily. Azathioprine (Imuran) (50 mg three times a day)
was subsequently added because of a waning response to
prednisone.
Repeated performance of a radioiodine (
131I) thyroid
uptake and scan revealed essentially normal findings.
Results of thyroid function tests were notably improved
(Table 1). At follow-up, the patient was taking azathio-
prine (150 mg/day) and prednisone (20 to 80 mg/day). She
remained clinically euthyroid, with dramatically
decreased symptoms of SPS. Incidentally, steroid-induced
diabetes developed about 1 year after her initial endocrine
evaluation, for which therapy with rosiglitazone (4 mg
twice a day) was begun.
Further evaluation revealed persistently positive anti-
GAD antibodies (>100 U/mL; normal, <1.5 U/mL) 18
months after the initial evaluation. The TRABs were TSI
248% and TBII <5 U/L. The patient was positive for
HLA-DQB1*0201/02 and 0201/02/03, HLA-DRB1*0301,
HLA-DRB1*0701, HLA-DRB3*01, and HLA-DRB4*04
antigens.
DISCUSSION
Graves’ disease is an autoimmune condition associat-
ed with positive TRABs in about 95% of patients (1,2).
SPS, a rare neurologic disorder of unknown cause, is char-
acterized by the presence of progressive painful spasms
and stiffness and rigidity of the axial and proximal leg
muscles. It is associated with characteristic EMG changes
and positive anti-GAD antibody serology in about 60% of
cases (4,10-13). SPS is thought to be attributable to an
autoimmune process because of the positive anti-GAD
antibodies; however, some cases of SPS are associated
with a paraneoplastic process (4,17-24), and others have
no discernible malignant involvement or positive anti-
GAD antibodies (4). Treatment of SPS is difficult; many
patients obtain symptomatic relief from benzodiazepines,
valproate, and baclofen (13,25,26). Other patients require
manipulation of the immune system for an appreciable
effect on the disease, including the use of IVIG (27,28),
plasmapheresis (29), and corticosteroids (30). GAD is the
rate-limiting enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of glu-
tamic acid into the inhibitory neurotransmitter γ-aminobu-
tyric acid (GABA). The loss of GABAergic input in motor
neurons is thought to result in tonic firing at rest and
excessive excitation in response to sensory stimuli (31).

It has been shown that the symptoms of SPS diminish
with use of GABA agonists (benzodiazepines) (26); in
addition, the continuous motor unit activity can be sup-
pressed by anesthesia and other central nervous system-
acting GABA agonists such as baclofen (9,32) and val-
proate (33). In vitro studies have demonstrated neutraliza-
tion of rat brain GAD activity with sera from patients with
SPS (34,35).
Moersch and Woltman (8) first described 14 patients
with SPS in 1956. None of the 14 patients had autoim-
mune disorders, but 4 had high basal metabolic rates,
which were ascribed to increased muscle activity.
Hyperthyroidism was ruled out. SPS has been associated
with autoimmune diseases—most commonly, type 1 dia-
betes. Ten percent of patients with SPS have associated
autoimmune thyroid disease, typically Hashimoto’s thy-
roiditis. Thirty percent of patients with SPS have type 1
diabetes, but 1 in 10,000 patients with type 1 diabetes
develops SPS. In patients with SPS, GAD antibody titers
are 50 to 500 times the levels found in patients with type
1 diabetes (31). The GAD antibodies seem to have differ-
ent functional epitopes in SPS and type 1 diabetes. The
GAD antibody in SPS apparently recognizes the confor-
mational site of enzymatic activity on GAD (31,36). It is
also associated with the presence of multiple auto-
antibodies, including thyroid microsomal antibodies
(4,10,11). It has been reported in association with hyper-
thyroidism and hypothyroidism (4,10-15), but it has never
been described in association with Graves’ disease in
which TRAB positivity has been reported.
In 1961, Werk et al (14) described a 44-year-old black
man with thyrotoxicosis and SPS. The cause of the thyro-
toxicosis was not stated, but it seemed likely that he had
Graves’ disease. He had classic symptoms of hyperthy-
roidism, had no Graves’ eye disease, but had a 35-g goiter
and localized pretibial myxedematous skin changes asso-
ciated with substantially increased radioiodine uptake.
LATS status was not determined. In an assessment of 33
patients with SPS, Solimena et al (10) found 20 to have
positivity for islet cell antibodies. Among patients positive
for anti-GAD antibodies, 3 were reported to have Graves’
disease with no further specific characterization, 9 of 19
had positive thyroid microsomal antibodies, and 4 of 15
had positive thyroglobulin antibodies. Lorish et al (15)
described one case of hyperthyroidism associated with

SPS among a cohort of 13 patients seen at the Mayo
Clinic. No further description was given about the hyper-
thyroidism.
Both Graves’ disease and SPS are associated with cer-
tain HLA haplotypes and immune markers. Graves’ dis-
ease is associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DQA1*0501
(causative) and HLA-DRB1*0701 (protective) (1,2).
HLA-DRB1*03, DRB1*08, DRB3*0101, and
DRB3*0202 are associated with Graves’ disease (37).
Both type 1 diabetes and SPS are associated with a high
frequency of HLA-DQB1*0201 allele (38). Our patient
was positive for both HLA-DQB1*0201 and HLA-
DRB1*03. Of interest, she also has HLA-DRB1*0701,
which is protective for Graves’ disease.
Our patient was treated with an aggressive course of
immunosuppression (high-dose prednisone and azathio-
prine) for her SPS, after which she became clinically and
biochemically euthyroid and remained so during immuno-
suppressive therapy. Immunosuppressive therapy has dif-
ferent effects on the course of Graves’ disease. Graves’
disease has developed in patients receiving immunosup-
pressive therapy for cardiac (39), renal (40), and liver
(41,42) transplantation and bone marrow transplantation
(43) as well as with the use of antithymocyte globulin for
aplastic anemia (44). Thomson et al (45) described a case
of Graves’ disease developing in a patient receiving
immunosuppressive therapy—prednisone (15 mg/day)
and azathioprine (100 mg/day)—for autoimmune
hemolytic anemia. Euthyroidism was achieved by admin-
istration of carbimazole, azathioprine, prednisone, and
propranolol. She had positive TBII, which decreased after
addition of carbimazole to the immunosuppressive
therapy. Thyroglobulin and microsomal antibodies were
negative.
Werner and Platman (46) described 5 patients with
Graves’ disease treated with high doses of prednisone (up
to 160 mg daily) for variable periods up to 2.5 months. All
had Graves’ eye disease. All patients showed clinical and
biochemical euthyroidism after prednisone therapy. One
patient had clearly positive LATS serology, which was
shown to decrease with use of prednisone therapy. Two
patients had borderline LATS serology, which normalized
in one and remained positive in the other after prednisone
therapy. Snyder et al (47) described the disappearance of
LATS in 2 patients with Graves’ disease and Graves’ eye
disease treated with high-dose prednisone. The response
of the LATS to prednisone parallels that of the Graves’
ophthalmopathy.
Cyclosporine, in a dosage of 5 mg/kg daily, reduced
thyroglobulin antibodies in one patient, which increased
after cessation of therapy. Moreover, a dosage of 10 mg/kg
daily reduced both thyroglobulin and microsomal antibod-
ies in another patient with Graves’ eye disease (48).
Perros et al (49) treated 10 euthyroid patients who had
Graves’ eye disease with azathioprine, 150 mg/day for a
year. In comparison with control subjects, azathioprine
significantly lowered both thyroid microsomal and TBII
antibody levels in these patients. Burrow et al (50), who
studied 5 patients with Graves’ eye disease, were able to
show that azathioprine (2 mg/kg) suppressed the immune
system. In addition, they showed that azathioprine low-
ered the LATS antibody levels in a euthyroid patient, from
212% to 144%.
Of interest, anti-GAD antibodies remained strongly
positive in our patient despite a notable decrease in neuro-
logic symptoms during immunosuppressive therapy. Thus,
the presence of anti-GAD antibodies may be an epiphe-

nomenon with no direct etiologic role in SPS. Our
patient’s TRABs were significantly changed by immuno-
suppression—TSI decreased from 1,986% to 248%
(~90%) and TBII normalized. This change might explain
the clinical and biochemical improvement in her Graves’
disease. Even though the TSI was not normal, this level
may represent a threshold effect. It is recognized that
asymptomatic and euthyroid patients can have positive
thyroid autoantibodies (4-7). Perhaps the differences in
Graves’ activity during immunosuppressive therapy are
due to variations in doses of the immunosuppressants. In
all the cited cases in which Graves’ disease went into
remission, high doses were used—as was the case in our
patient. In the setting of transplantation, usually lower
doses of the immunosuppressants are used.
CONCLUSION
We report a case of SPS associated with symptomatic
TRAB-positive Graves’ disease at diagnosis. Treatment of
the worsening SPS with azathioprine and prednisone sub-
stantially diminished the neurologic symptoms of our
patient. Coincident with this response was improvement of
her hyperthyroidism and results of thyroid function tests.
Most likely, her immunosuppressive therapy induced a
remission of her Graves’ disease. The immunobiologic
mechanisms of Graves’ disease are complex, and this case
adds to the complexities in our efforts to understand the
pathogenesis of Graves’ disease and other autoimmune
diseases, including SPS.

ABSTRACT
Objective: To report an association between two
autoimmune conditions, Graves’ disease and stiff-person
(stiff-man) syndrome, and discuss the relevant literature.
Methods: We present a case of a 52-year-old white
woman with stiff-person syndrome who also had Graves’
disease, discuss her management, and review the related
literature. Pertinent published reports from 1950 through
2004 were researched with use of MEDLINE and
PubMed, and cross-references to other articles were
reviewed.
Results: A 52-year-old white woman presented with
symptoms of hyperthyroidism due to Graves’ disease.
Laboratory data were as follows: thyrotropin <0.005
μIU/mL, thyroxine 11.1 μg/dL, free thyroxine index (FTI)
10.7, and triiodothyronine 170 ng/dL. Thyroid-stimulating
immunoglobulins (TSI) and thyrotropin-binding inhibito-
ry immunoglobulins (TBII) were positive at 1,986% and
82.5 U/L, respectively. The hyperthyroidism was treated
with propranolol. She had a long-standing history of mus-
culoskeletal complaints and was ultimately diagnosed
with stiff-person syndrome. During her thyroid evalua-
tion, she had severe neurologic deterioration that necessi-
tated hospitalization and treatment with clonazepam,
baclofen, intravenous immunoglobulin, and subsequently
prednisone and azathioprine for appreciable symptomatic
relief. The aggressive immunosuppression had a profound
effect on her symptoms of hyperthyroidism, results of thy-
roid function tests, and thyrotropin receptor antibodies
(TRABs). Thyrotropin was 0.52 μIU/mL, thyroxine was
6.9 μg/dL, and FTI was 5.7. The TSI decreased from
1,986% to 248%, and her TBII normalized from 82.5 U/L
to <5 U/L. She was clinically and biochemically euthyroid
at last follow-up in May 2004.
Conclusion: This case illustrates the association
between TRAB-positive Graves’ disease and stiff-person
syndrome and the improvement of Graves’ disease with
immunosuppressive therapy. (Endocr Pract. 2005;11:
259-264)
INTRODUCTION
Graves’ disease is a common autoimmune disorder
with an annual incidence of 80 cases per 100,000 in
women and 10 cases per 100,000 in men (1,2). The iden-
tification of the long-acting thyroid stimulator (LATS)
thyrotropin receptor as the target of the LATS IgG and
demonstration of the presence of thyrotropin receptor anti-
bodies (TRABs) in more than 95% of patients with
Graves’ disease indicate an autoimmune basis. The
strongest direct evidence comes from the stimulation of
thyroid cellular activity in vitro by IgG from patients with
Graves’ disease and the passive transfer of transient
hyperthyroidism to the newborn of an affected pregnant
mother (1,2). Graves’ disease is associated with many
organ-specific autoimmune conditions, including type 1
diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease, vitiligo, pernicious
anemia, myasthenia gravis, and premature ovarian failure
(2,3), as well as autoimmune antibody positivity even in
the absence of overt clinical disease (4-7).
Stiff-person (stiff-man) syndrome (SPS) is a rare neu-
rologic syndrome of unknown cause, characterized by
progressive painful muscle spasms, muscle stiffness, and
muscle rigidity (8,9). SPS is a clinical diagnosis, associat-
ed with positive anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)
antibodies and a suggestive electromyogram (EMG)
(4,10-13). SPS is associated with several autoimmune

CASE REPORT
A 52-year-old right-handed white woman presented
to the endocrine clinic for evaluation of hyperthyroidism.
She had a 9-month history of anxiety, rapid speech, dysp-
nea on exertion, generalized weakness, and tremulousness.
She had no local neck symptoms. She reported intermit-
tent fatigue, mood swings, restless sleep, heat intolerance,
and excessive sweating. She had also noticed palpitations
and had irregular menses. Although her appetite had
increased, she had maintained a stable weight. She had
some eyelid swelling and minimal discomfort. A review of
systems revealed considerable muscle aches and stiffness
in the back and legs, gait difficulties, frequent falls, diffi-
culty climbing stairs, and urinary incontinence. Her histo-
ry revealed hypertension, osteoarthritis with cervical and
lumbar spondylosis, cholecystectomy, and tubal ligation.
She reported a strong family history of Graves’ disease
(sister and first cousin). She was married and had 3 chil-
dren. She denied alcohol or tobacco use. Her drug history
included tolterodine (Detrol), sertraline (Zoloft), baclofen,
and lisinopril.
On physical examination, the patient’s weight was
82.1 kg, height was 165 cm, pulse was 84 beats/min, and
blood pressure was 210/90 mm Hg. She looked anxious,
with a stare, chemosis, and lid lag. The rest of the eye
examination, including exophthalmometry, showed no
other abnormalities. She had fine tremors of the out-
stretched hands; normal findings on thyroid examination;
brisk symmetric reflexes; proximal myopathy; abnormal
gait, almost spastic in nature; and spasm of the anterior
abdominal wall and paraspinal musculature. The rest of
her examination was unremarkable.
Initial thyroid function tests indicated biochemical
hyperthyroidism (Table 1). Radioiodine (
131I) thyroid
uptake was 16% at 4 hours (estimated as 33% at 24 hours),
and the scan showed a homogeneous pattern. TRABs were
positive (Table 1). Thyrotropin-binding inhibitory
immunoglobulins (TBII) were measured by radioreceptor
assay (Kronus, Inc.), and thyroid-stimulating immuno-
globulins (TSI) were measured by a cell bioassay, as
described previously (16). Treatment with propranolol (40
mg three times daily) was initiated.
Before her visit to the endocrine clinic, the patient had
had several consultations with specialists, including a
rheumatologist, spine orthopedist, pulmonologist, and
neurologist. She had an extensive evaluation, including
magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which showed
normal findings, and of the spine, which disclosed moder-
ate cervical and lumbar spondylosis without spinal cord
compromise. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(Westergren), C-reactive protein, serum protein elec-
trophoresis, and rheumatoid factor all demonstrated
normal results. She had normal chest x-ray findings and
restrictive physiology, with normal diffusion lung capaci-

activation of normal motor units of the paraspinal and
proximal lower extremity muscles.
The patient was diagnosed with SPS (elevated anti-
GAD antibody level, 431 nmol/L; normal, ≤0.02 nmol/L).
Treatment with baclofen yielded improvement in painful
spasms, and she had no further falls. Her ambulation was
substantially improved. Three months later, however, she
required hospitalization because of worsening dyspnea,
frequent falls, and increasing painful spasms. She was
treated with clonazepam (Klonopin) but had little
improvement. She received a 5-day course of intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy (400 mg/kg daily). An
echocardiogram showed normal findings, as did computed
tomographic scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
Subsequent improvement allowed her dismissal from the
hospital.
Within a month, deterioration of the patient’s condi-
tion necessitated another 5-day course of IVIG, which
yielded no improvement. She was then treated with a
5-day intravenous course of methylprednisolone at 1
g/day, and dramatic improvement ensued. She continued
with orally administered prednisone in dosages up to 80
mg daily. Azathioprine (Imuran) (50 mg three times a day)
was subsequently added because of a waning response to
prednisone.
Repeated performance of a radioiodine (
131I) thyroid
uptake and scan revealed essentially normal findings.
Results of thyroid function tests were notably improved
(Table 1). At follow-up, the patient was taking azathio-
prine (150 mg/day) and prednisone (20 to 80 mg/day). She
remained clinically euthyroid, with dramatically
decreased symptoms of SPS. Incidentally, steroid-induced
diabetes developed about 1 year after her initial endocrine
evaluation, for which therapy with rosiglitazone (4 mg
twice a day) was begun.
Further evaluation revealed persistently positive anti-
GAD antibodies (>100 U/mL; normal, <1.5 U/mL) 18
months after the initial evaluation. The TRABs were TSI
248% and TBII <5 U/L. The patient was positive for
HLA-DQB1*0201/02 and 0201/02/03, HLA-DRB1*0301,
HLA-DRB1*0701, HLA-DRB3*01, and HLA-DRB4*04
antigens.
